title: Pick it provisionally; Penstock and Runnymede undervalued
markdown:
**1. The chosen name.**

Countermand Labs maps one precise word onto the "human overrides risky AI action" half of the thesis. Clean at Companies House, all four domains free, no real namesake. Won 12/15 runs, usually by a clear margin.

But it covers only the override half — nothing for "capability granted" or "flows only where it may" — yet fit scored near-perfect almost unanimously: grading on vibes, not the criterion. It reads martially: judges flagged "rare-word risk" and command-tone while voting for it. "Labs" undersells a consultancy-led business, signalling R&D not delivery. Only Companies House and domains were checked, never trademarks.

I'd pick it, provisionally: memorable, sober, ownable by the evidence gathered, the decisive winner. But I'd run a trademark search and test the martial tone with real CISOs — the panel is confident on data it never checked.

**2. Other names you like.**

Claustra Labs is the runner-up: Latin containment gravitas nearer Palantir's register, covering the "flows only where it may" clause Countermand skips. Claustrophobia is a real objection but manageable.

The league undervalued two. Penstock Labs (0 wins) is the tightest metaphor in the field — a sluice gate governs how much flows and when, covering capability-granting and flow-control, better coverage than the winner. It lost mainly on unfamiliarity and a sound-alike to Pentera, a pen-testing firm in a different market — overweighted against what it buys. Runnymede Labs (0 wins) is distinctly British, weighty (Magna Carta, limits on power), fitting "UK founder-led, regulated sectors" better than anything proposed; overlap with the Runnymede Trust and council is a footnote, not a registration block.

**3. How effective the process was.**

What worked: the shared dossier caught real landmines early (Hadrian, Cordon, Chancery, Barbican, Corbel, Auctra, Aegis, Sentinel — all blocked or saturated), and the planted control died round 1 every time, proving the panel discriminates. Fifteen repeats surfaced a real signal a single run couldn't.

The measures are less flattering. Effective-judges collapses to ~1.1-1.3 of ten (round-1 correlation 0.88-0.90); restricted to Companies-House-clear names, correlation still sits at 0.74-0.77 — ten models act as barely more than one judge, agreeing on shared facts, not taste. Jev, meant as an independent check, correlates 0.97 with the panel — reinforcing consensus, not diversifying it. Self-preference is real but uneven: claude-sonnet-5 is self-critical (-0.36) and the most accurate judge (0.81); gpt-5.6-luna (+0.66) and claude-haiku-4.5 (+0.56) inflate their own entries and judge worse (0.77, 0.71). Herding toward the shared mean is near zero to slightly negative, but round-to-round movement (~0.46-0.49) exceeds the final margin between the top two (0.13-0.26 in three Claustra wins).

Threats to validity: the shared dossier plus a mechanical ownable score (25%, pass/fail on CH and domains) narrow what's judged; halving 31 candidates to 16 in one noisy round risks cutting a good name on bad luck; similar-tier models compound correlation beyond the dossier; and backing reward goes flat at 1 point for rounds 5-7, so late leader-following pays like early conviction, as the data shows.

**4. One change you'd make first.**

Replace Jev with a different evaluator — a human panel, or a model briefed adversarially, not handed the judges' own brief. At 0.97 correlation, Jev buys a second vote for the same opinion, not independence. That gap must close before adversarial panels can be trusted as a method.

title: Shortlist it, don't pick it yet
markdown:
## 1. The chosen name

**Countermand Labs** fits the brief well. It names the one thing competitors can't easily claim: a person's authority to stop an agent. It's a real English word, easy to spell, sober, and every checked domain is free. The risks:
- **It's negative and military.** It names a brake, not what the firm builds. The company sells working applications, and "Countermand" suggests a firm that overrules its clients' orders. Judges raised the military tone in every final.
- **"Labs" works against the gravitas.** It sounds experimental to a CFO. It's also why the name came back clear: the bare word "Countermand" was never checked at Companies House, for domains, or at UKIPO.
- **It isn't wry.** The brief asked for "a little wry", and no criterion scored that.

I'd shortlist it but not pick it yet. First I'd run a UKIPO check and test it on 5–10 real CFOs and CISOs for recall after one hearing. The league can't measure memorability, however many times it runs.

## 2. Other names you like

- **Penstock.** A penstock is a sluice gate that meters a river, which is controlled flow, and it sounds civilian and engineered. The league undervalued it. "Pentera" is a weak sound-alike, and Penstock Group is US healthcare software, a different field.
- **Chary.** It's the only name that's actually wry, and it's short and ownable. Worries that people would read it as "charity" cost it more than they should have.
- **Imprimatur.** It means official approval, which is exactly "waits for human sign-off", and it has real weight. The Catholic-censorship association is a real cost, but a small one for this audience.
- **Countersign** (not in the league, unchecked). It means a second signature before an action goes ahead, which is the human-approval step put positively. Worth checking against Countermand.

## 3. How effective the process was

**What worked:**
- It cheaply cut 31 names to a sensible top six for $7.
- The dossier removed names that are unusable (blocked or crowded).
- Critiques were specific.

**What the measures actually show:**
- **Judge correlation.** It was 0.88, which works out to about 1.1 effective judges, or 1.3 counting only names that were legally clear. Ten models behaved like one judge, and mostly they were agreeing with the dossier. Critiques often repeat its wording, e.g. "military tone" and "Pentera".
- **Herding.** About 0 in all variants. Judges rescored by around 0.46 points, but not towards the shared mean. That's reassuring, but narrow: it doesn't measure influence from critiques or advocates.
- **Jev.** Correlation with the panel was 0.97, so giving Jev the same weight as the whole panel added no independent information. Variant B went 5–0 to Countermand, which fits Jev amplifying the consensus.
- **Backing.** Models picked the previous round's leader 3 or 4 times out of 4. That's following momentum, not prediction. With a flat 16/8/4/2/1 reward, the best strategy is to copy the leader.
- **"Judge accuracy."** It's circular: it measures agreement with a final order that the judges themselves produced.
- **Self-preference.** Low on average (0.11–0.13), but 0.66 for gpt-5.6-luna and 0.56 for claude-haiku-4.5. Those scores were already dropped from the tally.
- **Control.** It went out in round 1 every time. That only tests the floor: a generic name with no free domains is easy to kill. It says nothing about telling the top names apart.

**Threats to validity:**
- **Not real replications.** The same two names reached all 15 finals. All runs shared one candidate pool and one dossier, so they are resamples of the same models, not replications. Variant C's 3–2 against A/B's 9–1 is too small a sample to mean anything.
- **Shared dossier.** One research pass settled ownability for every judge and included opinions ("strong military connotation"). Any error in it reached every judge.
- **Similar models.** They share training priors that favour Latin and archaic words. No human judged anything.
- **Halving by mean score.** It cuts names that split opinion, and the result was effectively fixed in round 1 (8.06 vs 7.90).
- **Rubric weights.** "Fit" at 30% rewards names that describe the thesis literally. There was no criterion for wryness or trademark risk.
- **"Labs" suffix.** Almost every "Labs" name came back clear and 11 of 16 bare names were blocked or at risk. That tilted ownability scores, which count for 25%.

## 4. One change you'd make first

Check every name both bare and with "Labs", and give judges a dossier of facts only (registry results, domains, named clashes) with no evaluative wording. At present the dossier and the suffix settle most of the result before any judging starts. Until that's fixed, the extra runs, variants and metrics are measuring one research pass, not ten judges.

title: Defensible, but the dossier did half the judging
markdown:
## 1. The chosen name

Countermand Labs is a defensible pick. Strengths: it names the mechanism (a human revoking an agent's order) rather than a shield metaphor; it is a real word a CFO knows, spellable after one hearing, with Companies House and all four domains clear. Weaknesses: it is stern, not wry; every final critique flagged the command-and-control register, and it sells the brake, not the car; "Labs" is a startup suffix for a firm wanting £100m gravitas, and bare countermand.* was never checked. It also won a thin field: 31 LLM-generated names, mostly Latin or medieval words plus "Labs", 13 registrable. I would pick it over anything else here because it states the thesis in one ordinary word, but only after five real CISOs hear it cold.

## 2. Other names you like

- **Penstock Labs**: the best controlled-flow metaphor, industrial and British. Undervalued: third by round-1 mean yet never in a final, because the Pentera sound-alike was charged twice (ownable and distinct) although Pentera sells pen-testing to a different buyer.
- **Runnymede Labs**: power accepting limits; the strongest story for a regulated CFO. The Runnymede Trust and missing .com are real costs, fairly priced.
- **Imprimatur Labs**: approval at its purest; censorship over-penalised, the UK Imprimatur Group under-penalised.
- Off-league, worth a dossier: **Remit**, one's granted scope of authority, wry and British.

## 3. How effective the process was

What worked: blind judging, dropped own-name scores, the planted control and 15 repeats, enough to show 12/15, not 15/15, with variant C flipping twice. The measures are less flattering. Judge correlation 0.88 (0.76 on clear names) gives 1.1 to 1.3 effective judges: ten models are one judge. Jev at 0.97 with the panel adds cost, not information. Herding near zero is not independence; there was no disagreement left to herd. Self-preference of 0.11 to 0.13 is small but skewed (luna 0.66, haiku 0.56, sonnet -0.36). Backing: every judge picks the previous leader 3 or 4 times in 4, so the 16/8/4/2/1 reward measures leader-following; with the leader visible after round 1 it is effectively flat. "Judge accuracy" is correlation with an order the judge helped produce: gpt-oss at 0.68 is least conformist, not least accurate. The control's round-1 exit clears a low bar.

Threats to validity: the shared dossier is the dominant input; ownable (25%) plus the clash half of distinct are that dossier read back as numbers, and with 14 names blocked or domainless the real contest was three rounds among eight. Ownability was checked on whatever form the proposer typed: bare Seneschal had no domains, Seneschal Labs had four, and the top nine all carry the suffix, so the suffix decided a quarter of the score. With similar models, halving by mean score is halving by one judge, and showing last round's panel mean makes the top two sticky. Wryness and one-hearing recall are unscored.

## 4. One change you'd make first

Pre-screen ownability mechanically (blocked or no usable domain is out; research bare and suffixed forms), drop it from the rubric, and spend the panel on 60 or more clear names from more diverse generators, humans included. Half the current signal is paperwork transcribed by one effective judge; only three rounds among eight names mattered. Choosing only among registrable names makes the tournament measure taste rather than availability.
